A $1m$ long copper wire carries a current of $1A$. If the cross section of the wire is $2 . 0{mm}^{2}$ and the resistivity of copper is $1 . 7 \times {10}^{- 8}Ωm$. The force experienced by moving electron in the wire is _____$\times {10}^{- 23}N$

(Charge of electron$= 1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19}C$ )
questions.explanation:
Given here, length $l = 1m$, current $i = 1A$, area $A = 2 \times {10}^{- 6}m$ and resistivity $ρ = 1 . 7 \times {10}^{- 8}Ωm$.

Resistance of wire is $R = \dfrac{ρl}{A} = \dfrac{1 . 7 \times {10}^{- 8} \times 1}{2 \times {10}^{- 5}} = \dfrac{1 . 7}{2} \times {10}^{- 2}Ω$

Now, electric field in the wire is $E = ρJ$, where, $J = \dfrac{i}{A}$ is current density.

Thus, $E = \dfrac{iρ}{A} = iR = 1 \times \dfrac{1 . 7}{2} \times {10}^{- 2}V{m}^{- 1}$

Electric force in terms of electric field is given by $F = qE$

Therefore, force experienced by moving electron is $F = 1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19} \times \dfrac{1 . 7}{2} \times {10}^{- 2}$

$= 1 . 36 \times {10}^{- 21}$= 136 \times {10}^{- 23}N$

questions.q: A long cylindrical volume contains a uniformly distributed charge of density $ρC{m}^{- 3}$. The electric field inside the cylindrical volume at a distance $x = \dfrac{2{ε}_{0}}{ρ}m$ from its axis is _____ $V{m}^{- 1}$.
questions.solution:
Given here, Volume charge density $= ρC{m}^{- 3}$.

Consider a Gaussian cylindrical surface of height $h$ and radius $x$.

Let $q$ charge is enclosed by the cylinder of radius $x$.

From Gauss's law,

$∫ E d Scos0 = \dfrac{q}{{ε}_{0}}$

Here, $q =$volume charge density$\times$volume of imaginary cylinder.

$⇒ E\left(2\pixh\right) = \dfrac{ρ \times \pi{x}^{2}h}{{ε}_{0}}$

$⇒ E = \dfrac{ρx}{2{ε}_{0}}$

$⇒ E = \dfrac{ρ}{2{ε}_{0}} \times \dfrac{2{ε}_{0}}{ρ} = 1$

Thus, electric field is $1V{m}^{- 1}$.

questions.q: Two uniformly charged spherical conductors $A$ and $B$ of radii $5mm$ and $10mm$ are separated by a distance of $2cm$. If the spheres are connected by a conducting wire, then in equilibrium condition, the ratio of the magnitudes of the electric fields at the surface of the sphere $A$ and $B$ will be
questions.solution:
When two conductors are connected by a conducting wire, their potentials become equal. Therefore, ${V}_{A} = {V}_{B}$

The potential of a spherical conductor is given by, $V = \dfrac{kQ}{R}$

$⇒ \dfrac{k{Q}_{A}}{{R}_{A}} = \dfrac{k{Q}_{B}}{{R}_{B}}$

$⇒ Q ∝ R$

Now the electric field near the surface of the conductor will be, $E = \dfrac{kQ}{{R}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{E}_{A}}{{E}_{B}} = \dfrac{k{Q}_{A}{R}_{A}^{2}}{k{Q}_{B}{R}_{B}^{2}} = \dfrac{{R}_{B}}{{R}_{A}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{E}_{A}}{{E}_{B}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

questions.q: Three point charges of magnitude $5\muC, 0 . 16\muC$ and $0 . 3\muC$ are located at the vertices $A, B, C$ of a right angled triangle whose sides are $AB = 3cm$, $BC = 3\sqrt{2}cm$ and $CA = 3cm$ and point $A$ is the right angle corner. Charge at point $A$ experiences _____ $N$ of electrostatic force due to the other two charges.
questions.solution:
Using Coulomb's law the electrostatic force on& $A$~due to& $C$

${F}_{AC} = \dfrac{K{q}_{A}{q}_{C}}{\left({r}_{AC}\right)2} = \dfrac{k \times 5 \times 0 . 3 \times {10}^{- 12}}{9 \times {10}^{- 4}}= \dfrac{9 \times {10}^{9} \times 5 \times 0 . 3 \times {10}^{- 12}}{9 \times {10}^{- 4}}$

$= 1 . 5 \times 10 = 15N$

Similarly, the force on~$A$~due to& $B$

${F}_{AB} = \dfrac{K{q}_{A}{q}_{B}}{\left({r}_{AB}\right)2} = \dfrac{9 \times {10}^{9} \times 5 \times 0 . 16 \times {10}^{- 12}}{9 \times {10}^{- 4}} = 8N$

We can see that the forces are perpendicular to each other. Therefore, the net force experienced by charge at $A$~is,

$F = \sqrt{{FAC}^{2} + {FAB}^{2}}= \sqrt{{15}^{2} + {8}^{2}} = \sqrt{289} = 17N$

$= 45 \times {10}^{10}N{C}^{- 1}$

questions.q: Two point charges $Q$ each are placed at a distance $d$ apart. A third point charge $q$ is placed at a distance $x$ from mid-point on the perpendicular bisector. The value of $x$ at which charge $q$ will experience the maximum Coulomb's force is:
questions.solution:
The distance between $q$ and $Q$ is $r = \sqrt{{x}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)}^{2}} = \sqrt{{x}^{2} + \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4}}$.

The force between $q$ and $Q$ will be $F = \dfrac{kqQ}{{r}^{2}}$.

From the given figure we can see that only vertical components of the forces will add, and the horizontal components will get cancelled out. Therefore,

${F}_{net} = \dfrac{2kqQ}{{r}^{2}}cos\theta = \dfrac{2kqQ}{{r}^{2}} \times \dfrac{x}{r} = \dfrac{kqQx}{{\left({x}^{2} + \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4}\right)}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}}$

For force to be maximum, $\dfrac{d {F}_{net}}{d x} = 0 .$

$⇒ kqQ\left[\dfrac{\left({x}^{2} + \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4}\right)\dfrac{3}{2} - x \times \dfrac{3}{2}\left({x}^{2} + \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4}\right)\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2x}{{\left(\left({x}^{2} + \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4}\right)\dfrac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}}\right] = 0$

$⇒ \left({x}^{2} + \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4}\right) = 3{x}^{2} ⇒ 2{x}^{2} = \dfrac{{d}^{2}}{4} ⇒ x = \dfrac{d}{2\sqrt{2}}$

questions.q: If the electric potential at any point $\left(x, y, z\right)m$ in space is given by $V = 3{x}^{2}$ volt. The electric field at the point $\left(1, 0, 3\right)m$ will be :
questions.solution:
Electric potential $V = 3{x}^{2}$

Electric potential and electric field are related as $E = - \dfrac{d V}{d x} = - 6x$.

At the point $\left(1, 0, 3\right)m$,

$⇒ E = - 6 \times 1 = - 6V{m}^{- 1}$

Thus, electric field is $6V{m}^{- 1}$ along negative $x ‐$ axis.

questions.q: A positive charge particle of $100mg$ is thrown in opposite direction to a uniform electric field of strength $1 \times {10}^{5}N{C}^{- 1}$. If the charge on the particle is $40\muC$ and the initial velocity is $200{ms}^{- 1}$, how much distance it will travel before coming to the rest momentarily
questions.solution:
Force experienced by a particle with charge $q$ in an electric field $F = qE$.

Now, the acceleration produced is given as $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{qE}{m}$= \dfrac{40 \times {10}^{- 6} \times {10}^{5}}{1 \times {10}^{- 4}}$

$= 4 \times {10}^{4}m{s}^{- 2}$ (As the particle is projected against the electric field, hence it is decelerated)

Using, ${v}^{2} = {u}^{2} - 2as$

We have, ${0}^{2} = {u}^{2} - 2as$

$s = \dfrac{{v}^{2}}{2a} = \dfrac{{\left(200\right)}^{2}}{2 \times 4 \times {10}^{4}} = 0 . 5m$

Statement-I : A point charge is brought in an electric field. The value of electric field at a point near to the charge may increase if the charge is positive.

Statement-II : An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field. The net electric force on the dipole will not be zero.
options: Both statement-I and statement-II are true.
Both statement-I and statement-II are false.
Statement-I is true but statement-II is false.
Statement-I is false but statement-II is true.
questions.solution:
If a positive point charge is brought in an electric field. The value of electric field at a point near to the charge may increase or decreases. Hence, statement I is true.

An electric dipole experiences zero net force in a uniform electric field. Hence, statement II is false.

questions.q: Two identical charged particles each having a mass $10g$ and charge $2 . 0 \times {10}^{- 7}C$ are placed on a horizontal table with a separation of $L$ between them such that they stay in limited equilibrium. If the coefficient of friction between each particle and the table is $0 . 25$, find the value of $L$. [Use $g = 10{ms}^{- 2}$ ]
questions.solution:
Normal reaction applied by table on object will be, $N = mg$.

Both charges are same, hence a repulsive force will act between them.

Value of force acting will be, $\dfrac{k{Q}^{2}}{{L}^{2}}$.

Now the maximum value of friction force which table can provide is,

$= \muN = \mumg$

For equilibrium, $\dfrac{k{Q}^{2}}{{L}^{2}} = \mumg$.

$L = \sqrt{\dfrac{k{Q}^{2}}{\mumg}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{0 . 25mg}}Q = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{mg}}Q$

$= 2\sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times {10}^{9}}{10 \times {10}^{- 3} \times 10}}\left(2 \times {10}^{- 7}\right) = 0 . 12m = 12cm$

(a) The electric lines of force entering into a Gaussian surface provide negative flux.
(b) A charge $q$ is placed at the centre of a cube. The flux through all the faces will be the same.
(c) In a uniform electric field net flux through a closed Gaussian surface containing no net charge, is zero.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
We know that electric flux is a scalar quantity and this is the scalar product of the magnitude of electric field and surface area.

Recall, the formula given by Gauss theorem, $ϕ = \overset{\to}{E} \cdot \overset{\to}{A} = EAcos\theta$, here $\theta = 90 °$, it means, $ϕ = 0$.

questions.q:
A particle of mass $1mg$ and charge $q$ is lying at the mid-point of two stationary particles kept at a distance $2m$ when each is carrying same charge $q$. If the free charged particle is displaced from its equilibrium position through distance $x \left(x < < 1m\right). The particle executes SHM. Its angular frequency of oscillation will be _______ $\times {10}^{5}rad{s}^{- 1}$ (if ${q}^{2} = 10{C}^{2}$)

$
questions.solution:
Net force on free charged particle,

$F = \dfrac{k{q}^{2}}{{\left(d + x\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{k{q}^{2}}{{\left(d - x\right)}^{2}}$

$F = - k{q}^{2}\left[\dfrac{4dx}{{\left({d}^{2} - {x}^{2}\right)}^{2}}\right]$

$a = - \dfrac{4k{q}^{2}d}{m}\left(\dfrac{x}{{d}^{4}}\right)$

$a = - \left(\dfrac{4k{q}^{2}}{m{d}^{3}}\right)x$

So, angular frequency

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{4k{q}^{2}}{m{d}^{3}}}$

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{4 \times 9 \times {10}^{9} \times 10}{1 \times {10}^{- 6} \times {1}^{3}}}$

$\omega = 6 \times {10}^{8}rad{sec}^{- 1}$

questions.q: The total charge enclosed in an incremental volume of $2 \times {10}^{- 9}{m}^{3}$ located at the origin is  $nC,$ if electric flux density of its field is found as$D = {e}^{- x}siny\overset{^}{i} - {e}^{- x}cosy\overset{^}{j} + 2z\overset{^}{k}C{m}^{- 2}$
questions.solution:
Electric flux density,

$\left(\overset{\to}{D}\right) = \dfrac{\text{charge}}{\text{Area}} \times \overset{^}{r} = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi{r}^{2}}\overset{^}{r} = {ϵ}_{0}\left(\dfrac{Q}{4\pi{ϵ}_{0}{r}^{2}}\overset{^}{r}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{E} = \overset{\to}{D}{ϵ}_{0} = \dfrac{{e}^{- x}siny\overset{^}{i} - {e}^{- x}cos ( \overset{^}{j} + 2z\overset{^}{k )}}{{ϵ}_{0}}$

Also, by Gauss's law,

$\dfrac{ρ}{{ϵ}_{0}} = \left(\dfrac{∂}{∂ x}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ y}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ z}\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \overset{\to}{E} = \left(\dfrac{∂}{∂ x}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ y}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ z}\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \overset{\to}{D}{ϵ}_{0}$

$⇒ ρ = \dfrac{∂}{∂ x}\left({e}^{- x}siny\right) + \dfrac{∂}{∂ y}\left(- {e}^{- x}cosy\right) + \dfrac{∂}{∂ z} ( 2z )$

$ρ = - {e}^{- x}siny + {e}^{- x}siny + 2$
At origin $ρ = - {e}^{- 0}sin0 + {e}^{- 0}sin0 + 2$
$ρ = 2C{m}^{- 3}$

Charge $= ρ \times$ volume $= 2 \times 2 \times {10}^{- 9} = 4 \times {10}^{- 9} =$
$4nC$

$\dfrac{ρ}{{ϵ}_{0}} = \left(\dfrac{∂}{∂ x}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ y}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ z}\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \overset{\to}{E} = \left(\dfrac{∂}{∂ x}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ y}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{∂}{∂ z}\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \overset{\to}{D}{ϵ}_{0}$

$⇒ ρ = \dfrac{∂}{∂ x}\left({e}^{- x}siny\right) + \dfrac{∂}{∂ y}\left(- {e}^{- x}cosy\right) + \dfrac{∂}{∂ z} ( 2z )$

$ρ = - {e}^{- x}siny + {e}^{- x}siny + 2$
At origin $ρ = - {e}^{- 0}sin0 + {e}^{- 0}sin0 + 2$
$ρ = 2C{m}^{- 3}$

Charge $= ρ \times$ volume $= 2 \times 2 \times {10}^{- 9} = 4 \times {10}^{- 9} =$
$4nC$

questions.q: A certain charge $Q$ is divided into two parts $q$ and $( Q - q ) .$ How should the charges $Q$ and $q$ be divided so that $q$ and $( Q - q )$ placed at a certain distance apart experience maximum electrostatic repulsion?
questions.solution:
${F}_{q} = \dfrac{kq ( Q - q )}{{L}^{2}} = \dfrac{k}{{L}^{2}}\left(qQ - {q}^{2}\right)$
$\dfrac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}q} = 0$ when force is maximum
$\dfrac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}q} = \dfrac{k}{{L}^{2}} [ Q - 2q ] = 0$
$⇒ Q - 2q = 0 ⇒ Q = 2q$

questions.q: $27$ similar drops of mercury are maintained at $10V$ each. All these spherical drops combine into a single big drop. The potential energy of the bigger drop is ___________ times that of a smaller drop.
questions.solution:
$\left(27\right)\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi{r}^{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{R}^{3}$

$R = 3r$

Potential energy of smaller drop ${U}_{1} = \dfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{k{q}^{2}}{r}$

Potential energy of bigger drop : $U = \dfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{k{Q}^{2}}{R}$

$U = \dfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{k{\left(27q\right)}^{2}}{R}$

$U = \dfrac{3}{5}k\dfrac{\left(27\right)\left(27\right){q}^{2}}{3r}$

$U = \dfrac{\left(27\right)\left(27\right)}{3}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{k{q}^{2}}{r}\right)$

$U = 243{U}_{1}$

questions.solution:
$\overset{\to}{E} = \left(\dfrac{3{E}_{0}}{5}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{4{E}_{0}}{5}\overset{^}{j}\right)N{C}^{- 1}$

${A}_{1} = 0 . 2{m}^{2}$ [parallel to $y - z$ plane]

${A}_{2} = 0 . 3{m}^{2}$ [parallel to $x - z$ plane]

$\overset{\to}{A}2 = 0 . 3{m}^{2}\overset{^}{j}$

Now, ${ϕ}_{a} = \left[\dfrac{3{E}_{0}}{5}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{4{E}_{0}}{5}\overset{^}{j}\right] \cdot \left[0 . 2\overset{^}{i}\right] = \dfrac{3 \times 0 . 2}{5}{E}_{0}$

$\text{ and } {ϕ}_{b} = \left[\dfrac{3{E}_{0}}{5}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{4{E}_{0}}{5}\overset{^}{j}\right] \cdot \left[0 . 3\overset{^}{j}\right] = \dfrac{4 \times 0 . 3}{5}{E}_{0}$

Now, $\dfrac{{ϕ}_{a}}{{ϕ}_{b}} = \dfrac{0 . 6}{1 . 2} = \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{a}{b}$

$⇒ a: b = 1: 2$

$⇒ a = 1$

questions.q: A solid sphere of radius $R$ carries a charge $Q + q$ distributed uniformly over its volume. A very small point like piece of it of mass $m$ gets detached from the bottom of the sphere and falls down vertically under gravity. This piece carries charge $q$. questions.solution:
By using total energy conservation
$\DeltaKE + ( \DeltaPE{)}_{\text{electo}} + ( \DeltaPE{)}_{\text{gravitation}} = 0$

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{V}^{2} + \left(k\dfrac{Qq}{R + y} - k\dfrac{Qq}{R}\right) + ( - mgy ) = 0$

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{V}^{2} = mgy + kQq\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R + y}\right); {V}^{2} = 2gy + \dfrac{2kQq}{m}\dfrac{y}{R ( R + y )}$

${V}^{2} = 2y\left[\dfrac{qQ}{4\pi{ε}_{0}R ( R + y ) m} + g\right]$

questions.q: A two point charges $4q$ and $– q$ are fixed on the $x$ -axis at $x = \dfrac{- d}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{d}{2}$, respectively. If the third point charge ‘$q$ ’ is taken from the origin to $x = d$ along the semicircle as shown in the figure, the energy of the charge will:
questions.solution:
Potential at origin $O$, the potential due to two charges is given by

${V}_{0} = \dfrac{4q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)} + \dfrac{\left(- q\right)}{4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{6q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}d}$

Potential at $P$ at a distance, $x = d$ is given by

${V}_{P} = \dfrac{4q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{3d}{2}\right)} + \dfrac{\left(- q\right)}{4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{q}{6\pi{ε}_{0}d}$

Change in potential energy due the charge motion of charge $q$ is given by

$∆ U = q\DeltaV = q\left({V}_{f} - {V}_{i}\right)$

$⇒ ∆ U = q\left({V}_{P} - {V}_{O}\right)$

$∆ U = q\left(\dfrac{q}{6\pi{ε}_{0}d} - \dfrac{3q}{2\pi{ε}_{0}d}\right) = - \dfrac{4{q}^{2}}{3\pi{ε}_{0}d}$

questions.q: Concentric metallic hollow spheres of radii R and 4R hold charges ${Q}_{1}$ and ${Q}_{2}$ respectively. Given that surface charge densities of the concentric spheres are equal, the potential difference $V\left(R\right) - V ( 4R )$ is:
questions.solution:
As given the surface charge density for both the spheres is same, hence

${\sigma}_{1} = {\sigma}_{2} ∴ \dfrac{{Q}_{1}}{{A}_{1}} = \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{A}_{2}} ⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{1}}{4\pi{R}^{2}} = \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{4\pi{\left(4R\right)}^{2}} ∴ {Q}_{2} = 16{Q}_{1}$

From above diagram, the electric potential for both the spheres is

${V}_{Inner} = \dfrac{{KQ}_{1}}{R} + \dfrac{{KQ}_{2}}{4R} = \dfrac{K}{R}\left({Q}_{1} + \dfrac{16{Q}_{1}}{4}\right) = \dfrac{5{KQ}_{1}}{R} .$

In the same way for outer sphere,

${V}_{Outer} = \dfrac{{KQ}_{1}}{4R} + \dfrac{{KQ}_{2}}{4R} = \dfrac{K}{4R}\left(16{Q}_{1} + {Q}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{17{KQ}_{1}}{4R}$.

Now the potential difference is,

$∆ V = {V}_{inner} - {V}_{outer}$

$= \dfrac{5{KQ}_{1}}{R} - \dfrac{17{KQ}_{1}}{4R} = \dfrac{3{Q}_{1}}{16{\pi ε}_{0}R}$.

questions.q: An electric dipole of moment $\overset{\to}{\text{p}} = \left(- \overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}\right) \times {10}^{- 29}\text{C m}$ at the origin $\left(0,0, 0\right)$ . The electric field due to this dipole at $\overset{\to}{\text{r}} = + \overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + 5\overset{^}{k}$ (note that $\overset{\to}{r} ∙ \overset{\to}{p} = 0$ ) is parallel to:
questions.solution:
As $\overset{\to}{r} \cdot \overset{\to}{p} = 0$, this means that $\overset{\to}{r}$ is perpendicular to $\overset{\to}{p}$.

For an electric dipole, electric field at equatorial position is antiparallel to $\overset{\to}{p}$.

$⇒ \overset{\to}{E} = - \lambda\overset{\to}{p}$,

where, $\lambda$ is an arbitrary positive constant.

$⇒ \overset{\to}{E} = - \lambda\left(- \overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}\right) \times {10}^{- 29}C{m}^{- 2}$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{E} = \lambda\left(\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}\right) \times {10}^{- 29}C{m}^{- 2}$

For $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{{10}^{- 29}}$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{E} = \left(\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}\right)C{m}^{- 2}$

questions.q: In finding the electric field using Gauss law the formula $\left|\overset{\to}{E}\right| = \dfrac{{q}_{enc}}{{ε}_{0}\left|A\right|}$ is applicable. In the formula ${ε}_{0}$ is permittivity of free space, $A$ is the area of Gaussian surface and ${q}_{enc}$ is charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface. This equation can be used in which of the following situation?
options: Only when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface
Only when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface and $\left|\overset{\to}{E}\right|$ is constant on the surface.
Only when $\left|\overset{\to}{E}\right| =$ constant on the surface.
For any choice of Gaussian surface.
questions.solution:
According to Gauss law of electrostatics, the electric flux through an enclosed surface is given by ${ϕ}_{E} = \dfrac{{q}_{enc}}{{ε}_{0}}$

From the formula of electric flux, $ϕ = \overset{\to}{E} \cdot d \overset{\to}{s}$

Also, the relation between electric field and electric potential is given by $V = \overset{\to}{E} \cdot d \overset{\to}{r}$

So, the formula $\left|\overset{\to}{E}\right| = \dfrac{{q}_{enc}}{{ε}_{0}\left|A\right|}$ is only applicable when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface and $\left|\overset{\to}{E}\right|$ is constant on the surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ has an initial velocity $\overset{\to}{v} = {v}_{0}\overset{^}{j}$ . If an electric field $\overset{\to}{E} = {E}_{0}\overset{^}{i}$ and magnetic field $\overset{\to}{B} = {B}_{0}\overset{^}{i}$ act on the particle, its speed will double after a time
questions.solution:
Acceleration produced by electric field,
$a = \dfrac{q{E}_{0}}{m}\overset{^}{i}$

After time $t$, velocity of the particle,
$v = u + at$

$⇒ v = {v}_{0}\overset{^}{j} + \left(\dfrac{q{E}_{0}t}{m}\right)$\overset{^}{i}$\left[∵ u = v = {v}_{0}\overset{^}{j}\right]$

So, speed of the particle,
$\left|v\right|$ = \sqrt{{v}_{0}^{2} + {$\left(\dfrac{q{E}_{0}t}{m}\right)$}^{2}}$

Now, given \left|v\right| = 2{v}_{0}$after time $t$, so
$2{v}_{0} = \sqrt{{v}_{0}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{q{E}_{0}t}{m}\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ 4{v}_{0}^{2} = {v}_{0}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{q{E}_{0}t}{m}\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ 3{v}_{0}^{2} = {\left(\dfrac{q{E}_{0}t}{m}\right)}^{2}$

So, time interval, $t = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}m{v}_{0}}{q{E}_{0}}$

Here, we must note that no change in magnitude of velocity is caused by a perpendicular magnetic field. So, we are not taking effect of magnetic field while calculating change in speed.

questions.q: Let a total charge $2Q$ be distributed in a sphere of radius $R,$ with the charge density given by $ρ ( r ) = kr,$ where $r$ is the distance from the centre. Two charges $A$ and $B$ , of $- Q$ each, are placed on diametrically opposite points, at equal distance, a, from the centre. If $A$ and $B$ do not experience any force, then:
questions.solution:
As total charge on sphere is $= 2Q$
$2Q = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{R}\left(kr\right)\left(4\pi{r}^{2}dr\right) ⇒ k{\pi r}^{4} = 2Q$
Charged enclosed in the sphere of radius $a$
$q = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{a}kr \times 4\pi{r}^{2}dr = k\pi{a}^{4}$
As force on $Q$ is zero
$\dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}} \times \dfrac{{Q}^{2}}{{\left(2a\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{k\pi{a}^{4}}{4\pi{ε}_{0} \times {a}^{2}} \times Q$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}^{2}}{4} = k\pi{a}^{4}Q$
$= {a}^{4}\left(\dfrac{2Q}{{R}^{4}}\right)Q$
${R}^{4} = 8{a}^{4} ⇒ R = {8}^{\dfrac{1}{4}}a$ or $a = {8}^{- \dfrac{1}{4}}R$

questions.q: A simple pendulum of length $L$ is placed between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor having electric field $E$ , as shown in figure. Its bob has mass $m$ and charge $q$ . The time period of the pendulum is given by:
questions.solution:
Two forces will be acting on the mass $m$, gravity force and force by the electric field.

Thus, the effective force $= \sqrt{{\left(qE\right)}^{2} + {\left(mg\right)}^{2}}$
From force equation, ${g}_{eff} = \sqrt{{g}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{qE}{m}\right)}^{2}}$
Time period of the pendulum is $\left(T\right) = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{{g}_{eff}}}$
$= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{{g}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{qE}{m}\right)}^{2}}}}$

questions.q:
In free space, a particle $A$ of charge $1\muC$ is held fixed at point $P$ . Another particle $B$ of the same charge and mass $4\mug$ is kept at a distance of $1mm$ from $P .$ If $B$ is released, then its velocity at a distance of $9mm$ from $P$ is:
[Take $\dfrac{1}{4\pi{ϵ}_{0}} = 9 \times {10}^{9}N{m}^{2}{C}^{- 2}$ ]
questions.solution:
From conservation in mechanical energy:
$- \DeltaP . E . = \DeltaK . E .$
$\dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}{\left(1 \times {10}^{6}\right)}^{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{{10}^{- 3}} - \dfrac{1}{9 \times {10}^{- 3}}\right] = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times {10}^{- 6} \times {V}^{2}$
$9 \times {10}^{9} \times {10}^{- 12}\left[\dfrac{8}{9 \times {10}^{- 3}}\right] = 2 \times {10}^{- 6} \times {V}^{2}$
${V}^{2} = 4 \times {10}^{6}$
$V = 2 \times {10}^{3}m{s}^{- 1}$

questions.q: Four point charges $- q, + q, + q$ and $- q$ are placed on y-axis at $y = - 2d, y = - d,$ and $y = + 2d,$ respectively. The magnitude of the electric field $E$ at a point on the x-axis at $x = D,$ with $D ≫ d,$ will behave as:
questions.solution:
The electric field at $P$ is superposition of the fields due to all four charges. The electric field due to the two $+ q$ charges is

${E}_{+ q} = \dfrac{Kq}{{D}^{2} + {d}^{2}}{cos ⁡ \theta}_{1} \times 2$
${E}_{- q} = \dfrac{Kq}{{D}^{2} + 4{d}^{2}}{cos ⁡ \theta}_{2} \times 2$
The field due to $+ q$ is towards right and the field due to $- q$ is towards left. Also ${\theta}_{1} \approx 0$ and ${\theta}_{2} \approx 0$ .
$∴ {E}_{net} = {E}_{+ q} - {E}_{- q} \approx \dfrac{Kq}{{D}^{2} + {d}^{2}} - \dfrac{Kq}{{D}^{2} + 4{d}^{2}}$
$= \dfrac{Kq3{d}^{2}}{\left({D}^{2} + {d}^{2}\right)\left({D}^{2} + 4{d}^{2}\right)} \approx \dfrac{3Kq{d}^{2}}{{D}^{4}}$
$E ∝ \dfrac{1}{{D}^{4}}$

questions.q: A solid conducting sphere, having a charge $Q,$ is surrounded by an uncharged conducting hollow spherical shell. Let the potential difference between the surface of the solid sphere and that of the outer surface of the hollow shell be $V .$ If the shell is now given a charge of $– 4Q,$ the new potential difference between the same two surfaces is:
questions.solution:
First condition:

Both conducting spheres are shown.
${V}_{in} - {V}_{out} = \left(\dfrac{KQ}{{r}_{1}}\right) - \left(\dfrac{KQ}{{r}_{2}}\right)$
$⇒ V = KQ\left(\dfrac{1}{{r}_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}}\right)$
Second condition:

Shell is now given charge $- 4Q$ .
${V}_{in} - {V}_{out} = \left(\dfrac{KQ}{{r}_{1}} - \dfrac{4KQ}{{r}_{2}}\right) - \left(\dfrac{KQ}{{r}_{2}} - \dfrac{4KQ}{{r}_{2}}\right)$
$= \dfrac{KQ}{{r}_{1}} - \dfrac{KQ}{{r}_{2}}$
$= KQ\left(\dfrac{1}{{r}_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}}\right) = V$

questions.q: Charges $- q and + q$, located at A and B$, respectively, constitute an electric dipole. Distance $AB = 2a$, $O$ is the mid point of the dipole and $OP$ is perpendicular to $AB$. A charge $Q$ is placed at $P$ where $OP = y and y ≫ 2a$. The charge $Q$ experiences an electrostatic force $F$. If $Q$ is now moved along the equatorial line to $P '$ such that $OP ' = $\left(\dfrac{y}{3}\right)$ the force on $Q$ will be close to $\left(\dfrac{y}{3} ≪ 2a\right)$
questions.solution:
Electric field intensity at the distance $y$ along the perpendicular bisector is

$\left|{E}_{1}\right| = \dfrac{KP}{{y}^{3}}$

So, force at distance $y$ on $Q$,

$F = Q ( {E}_{1} ) = Q\left(\dfrac{KP}{{y}^{3}}\right)$ ...$( 1 )$

$F ' = Q\dfrac{KP}{{\left(\dfrac{y}{3}\right)}^{3}}$ ...$( 2 )$

Dividing $\left(1\right)$ by $\left(2\right)$, we get,

$\dfrac{F '}{F} = {\left(3\right)}^{3}$

$∴ F ' = 27F$

questions.q: Four equal point charges $Q$ each are placed in the $xy$ plane at $\left(0, 2\right), \left(4, 2\right), \left(4, - 2\right)$ and $\left(0, - 2\right) . The work required to put a fifth charge$Q$ at the origin of the coordinate system will be:$
questions.solution:
Work done in bringing the fifth charge at origin is equal to change in the potential energy of the system of charges.

${W}_{ext} = \Delta U= {U}_{f} - {U}_{i}$ if ${U}_{i} = 0$ (assumed)

${W}_{ext} = {U}_{f} - 0= \left[\dfrac{KQ^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{KQ^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{KQ^{2}}{2\sqrt{5}} + \dfrac{KQ^{2}}{2\sqrt{5}}\right]

Hence, the work done in bringing the fifth charge at the origin is
${W}_{ext} = $\dfrac{Q^{2}}{4\pi{ε}_{0}} \left[1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right].$

questions.q:
A charge $Q$ is distributed over three concentric spherical shells of radii $a, b, c\left(a < b < c\right)$ such that their surface charge densities are equal to one another.

The total potential at a point at distance $r$ from their common centre, where $r < a,$ would be:
questions.solution:
Surface charge densities of all sphere is given as $\dfrac{{q}_{1}}{{a}^{2}} = \dfrac{{q}_{2}}{{b}^{2}} = \dfrac{{q}_{3}}{{c}^{2}} = constant$, where ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$ and ${q}_{3}$ is charge on sphere of radius $a$, $b$ and $c$ respectively.

${q}_{1} + {q}_{2} + {q}_{3} = Q$

${q}_{1} = \dfrac{{a}^{2} ( Q )}{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}$

${q}_{2} = \dfrac{{b}^{2} ( Q )}{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}$

${q}_{3} = \dfrac{{c}^{2}\left(Q\right)}{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}$

Potential at a point where $r < a$ is given as $V = \dfrac{K{q}_{1}}{a} + \dfrac{K{q}_{2}}{b} + \dfrac{K{q}_{3}}{c}$, where $K$ is a constant.

$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\left[Q\right]\left(\dfrac{a + b + c}{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}\right)$

A third identical conducting sphere, $C$, is uncharged. Sphere $C$ is first touched to $A$, then to $B$, and then removed. As a result, the force between $A$ and $B$ would be equal to:
questions.solution:
$F = \dfrac{k{q}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}$ when $A$ and $C$ are touched charge on both will be $\dfrac{q}{2}$. Then when $B$ and $C$ are touched, ${q}_{B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{q}{2} + q}{2} = \dfrac{3q}{4}$

questions.q:
[12]
A solid ball of radius $\mathrm{R}$ has a charge density $\rho$ given by $\rho=\rho_0\left(1-\frac{r}{R}\right)$ for $0 \leq r \leq R$. The electric field outside the ball is:
options:
$\frac{\rho_0 R^3}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$

$\frac{4 \rho_0 R^3}{3 \varepsilon_0 r^2}$

$\frac{3 \rho_0 R^3}{4 \varepsilon_0 r^2}$

$\frac{\rho_0 R^3}{12 \varepsilon_0 r^2}$
questions.solution:
Charge density, $\rho=\rho_0 \left($1-$\frac{r}{R}\right)
\begin{aligned}
&d q=\rho d v \\
&q_{\text{in }}=\int d q=\rho d v \\
&=\rho_0\left(1-\frac{r}{R}\right) 4 \pi r^2 d r \quad\left(\because d v=4 \pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{dr}\right) \\
&=4 \pi \rho_0 \int_0^R\left(1-\frac{r}{R}\right) r^2 d r \\
&=4 \pi \rho_0 \int_0^R r^2 d r-\frac{r^2}{R} d r \\
&=4 \pi \rho_0\left[\left[\frac{r^3}{3}\right]_0^R-\left[\frac{r^4}{4 R}\right]_0^R\right] \\
&=4 \pi \rho_0\left[\frac{R^3}{3}-\frac{R^4}{4 R}\right]
\end{aligned}

$=4 $\pi \rho_$0$\left[\frac{R^3}{3}-\frac{R^3}{4}\right]=$4 $\pi \rho_$0$\left[\frac{R^3}{12}\right]$q=$\frac{\pi \rho_0 R^3}{3}
E .4 \pi r^2= \left(\frac{\pi \rho_0 R^3}{3 \epsilon_0}\right)\therefore \quad$ Electric field outside the ball, $E=\frac{\rho_0 R^3}{12 \in_0 r^2}$

questions.solution:
When cube is of side a and point charge $Q$ is at the center of the cube then the total electric flux due to this charge will pass evenly through the six faces of the cube. So, the electric flux through one face will be equal to $1 / 6$ of the total electric flux due to this charge.

questions.q: Three concentric metal shells $A, B$ and $C$ of respective radii $a, b$ and $c ( a < b < c )$ have surface charge densities $+ \sigma, - \sigma$ and $+ \sigma$ respectively. The potential of shell $B$ is:
questions.solution:
Net potential at B is due to the superposition of potential due to all shells,

${∨}_{B} = {∨}_{B\left(I\right)} + {∨}_{B\left(II\right)} + {∨}_{B\left(III\right)}$

$= \dfrac{K4\pi{a}^{2}\sigma}{b} + \dfrac{K4\pi{b}^{2}\left(- \sigma\right)}{b} + \dfrac{K4\pi{c}^{2}\left(\sigma\right)}{c}$

Required potential of b

$= \dfrac{\sigma{a}^{2}}{{ε}_{0}b} - \dfrac{\sigma{b}^{2}}{{ε}_{0}b} + \dfrac{\sigma{c}^{2}}{{ε}_{0}c}$

$= \dfrac{\sigma}{{ε}_{0}}\left(\dfrac{{{a}^{2} - b}^{2}}{b} + c\right)$

${\overset{\to}{T}}_{2} = - {\overset{\to}{T}}_{1}$

$∴ sin ⁡ \theta = \sqrt{3}cos ⁡ \theta$

$∴ tan ⁡ \theta = \sqrt{3}$

$∴ \theta = {60}^{o}$

questions.q:
The potential (in volts) of a charge distribution is given by

$V\left(z\right) = 30 - 5{z}^{2}$ for $\left|z\right| \le 1m$

$V\left(z\right) = 35 - 10\left|z\right|$ for $\left|z\right| \ge 1m$ .

$V\left(z\right) does not depend on x$ and y. If this potential is generated by a constant charge per unit volume{ρ}_{0}$ (in units of ${ϵ}_{0}$ ) which is spread over a certain region, then choose the correct statement.$
questions.solution:
Electric field due to given potentials is

${E}_{1} = \dfrac{- dV}{dz} = 10\left|z\right|$ for $∣ z ∣ \le 1m$. Here ${E}_{1}$ is proportional to $z$, so charge distribution is continuous for $\left|z\right| \le 1m$

${E}_{2} = - \dfrac{dV}{dz} = 10$ for $\left|z\right| \ge 1m$. Here, ${E}_{2}$ is constant.

So, using the Poisson’s equation ${∇}^{2}V = - \dfrac{ρ}{{ε}_{0}}$, we get $ρ = 0$.

$∴$ The source is an infinity large non-conducting thick plate.

Hence, consider a cylindrical Gaussian surface:

Applying Gauss's law for $∣ z ∣ \le 1m$

$E \times 2A = \dfrac{ρ \times 2z \times A}{{ε}_{0}}$

$⇒ \left(10z\right)\left(2A\right) = \dfrac{ρ ( 2Az )}{{ε}_{0}}$

$⇒ {ρ}_{0} = 10{ε}_{0}$ for $\left|z\right| \le 1m$.

questions.q: A thin disc of radius $b = 2a$ has a concentric hole of radius $a$ in it (see figure). It carries uniform surface charge $\sigma$ on it. If the electric field on its axis at a height $\text{h} \left(\text{h}< < \text{a}\right)$ from its centre is given as $\text{C}\text{h}$ then the value of $C$& is
questions.solution:
$∵$ At the axial point of a uniformly charged disc electric field is given by,

$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left(1 - cos\theta\right)$



By superposition principle, when inner disc is removed , then, electric field due to remaining disc is,



$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left[\left(1 - cos{\theta}_{2}\right) - \left(1 - cos{\theta}_{1}\right)\right]$

$= \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left[cos{\theta}_{1} - cos{\theta}_{2}\right]$

$= \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left[\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + {a}^{2}}} - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}\right]$

$= \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left[\dfrac{h}{a\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{{h}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}}} - \dfrac{h}{b\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{{h}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}}}\right]$

$∵ h ≪ a$ and b.

$∴ E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left[\dfrac{h}{a} - \dfrac{h}{b}\right]$

$= \dfrac{\sigma}{2{ϵ}_{0}}\left[\dfrac{h}{a} - \dfrac{h}{2a}\right] = \dfrac{\sigmah}{4{ϵ}_{0}a}$

$⇒ C = \dfrac{\sigma}{4{aϵ}_{0}}$.

questions.q:
Two long currents carrying thin wires, both with current $I$, are held by insulating threads of length L and are in equilibrium as shown in the figure, with threads making an angle ' $\theta$ ' with the vertical. If wires have a mass $\lambda$ per unit length then the value of $I$ is:
($g =$ gravitational acceleration)
questions.solution:
Two wires will repel each other due to magnetic force, then the magnetic force per unit length is,& $\dfrac{\text{d}\text{f}}{\text{d}\text{l}} = \dfrac{{μ}_{0}I^{2}}{2\pi\left(2\text{L}\text{sin}\theta\right)} = \dfrac{{μ}_{0}I^{2}}{4\pi\text{L}\text{sin}\theta}$. And mass per unit length of each wire$= \dfrac{\text{d}\text{m}}{\text{d}\text{l}} = \lambda$. So, the magnetic force on the total length $L$~of the wire is ${f}_{m} = \dfrac{{μ}_{0}I^{2}L}{4\pi\text{L}\text{sin}\theta}$, and weight $= \lambdaL\text{g}$. By equilibrium of wire, $\text{T}\text{sin}\theta = {f}_{m}\text{&}\text{T}\text{cos}\theta\text{=}\text{W}\text{=}\lambdal ' g⇒ \dfrac{\text{T}\text{sin}\theta}{\text{T}\text{cos}\theta} = \dfrac{\text{f}\text{m}}{mg} ⇒ {f}_{m} = \lambdal ' g tan \theta$
$⇒ \dfrac{{μ}_{0}I^{2}}{4\pi\text{L} sin \theta}L = \lambdaL\text{g}\dfrac{\text{sin}\theta}{\text{cos}\theta}$

$⇒ I^{2} = \dfrac{\lambda\text{g}\pi\text{L}}{{μ}_{0}\text{cos}\theta}4{sin}^{2}\theta\text{⇒}\text{I} = 2\text{sin}\theta\sqrt{\dfrac{\lambda\pi\text{gL}}{{μ}_{0}\text{cos}\theta}}$

questions.q:
A uniformly charged solid sphere of radius R has potential ${V}_{0}$ (measured with respect to $\infty$ ) on its surface. For this sphere the equipotential surfaces with potential $\dfrac{3{V}_{0}}{2}, \dfrac{5{V}_{0}}{4}, \dfrac{3{V}_{0}}{4}$ and $\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{4}$ have radius ${R}_{1}$ , ${R}_{2}, {R}_{3}$ and ${R}_{4}$ respectively. Then

Note : This question had two option correct at the time of examination. Proper corrections are made in the question to avoid it.
questions.solution:
Potential for uniformly charged solid sphere

$\text{v} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{r}}$ outside i.e r > R

$\text{v} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}}$ on the surface

$\text{v} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} \left[\dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{r}}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}}\right]$ inside i.e. r < R

Clearly

$\dfrac{3 {\text{v}}_{0}}{2} \text{,} \dfrac{5 {\text{v}}_{0}}{4}$ are inside potentials $\left[∵ > {\text{v}}_{0}\right]$

$\dfrac{3 {\text{v}}_{0}}{4} \text{,} \dfrac{{\text{v}}_{0}}{4}$ are outside potentials $\left[∵ < {\text{v}}_{0}\right]$

To get ${\text{R}}_{1}$: $\dfrac{3 {\text{v}}_{0}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} \left[\dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{1}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}}\right]$

${\text{where, v}}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}}$

$\dfrac{3}{2 \times 4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} \left[\dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{1}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}}\right]$

$\dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{1}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}} ⇒ {\text{R}}_{1} = 0$

To get ${\text{R}}_{2}$: $\dfrac{5}{4} {\text{v}}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} \left[\dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{2}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}}\right]$

$\dfrac{5}{4} \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} \left[\dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{2}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}}\right]$

$\dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{2}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{{\text{R}}_{2}^{2}}{{\text{R}}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4 }$⇒${\text{R}}_{2} = \dfrac{\text{R}}{\sqrt{2}}$

To get ${\text{R}}_{3}$ : $\dfrac{3 {\text{v}}_{0}}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{{\text{R}}_{3}}$

$\dfrac{3}{4} \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{{\text{R}}_{3}}$

$\dfrac{3}{4 \text{R}} = \dfrac{1}{{\text{R}}_{3}}$

${\text{R}}_{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \text{R}$

To get ${\text{R}}_{4}$: $\dfrac{{\text{v}}_{0}}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{{\text{R}}_{4}}$

$\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{\text{R}} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi {ε}_{0}} \dfrac{\text{Q}}{{\text{R}}_{4}}$

${\text{R}}_{4} = 4 \text{R}$

${\text{R}}_{4} - {\text{R}}_{3} = 4 \text{R} - \dfrac{4 \text{R}}{3} = \dfrac{8 \text{R}}{3} > {\text{R}}_{2}$

${\text{R}}_{1} = 0$ and ${\text{R}}_{2} < \left({\text{R}}_{4} - {\text{R}}_{3}\right)$

questions.q:
A spherically symmetric charge distribution is characterised by a charge density having the following variations:
$\rho(r)=\rho_o\left(1-\frac{r}{R}\right)$ for $r < R$\rho(\mathrm{r})=0$ for $r \geq \mathrm{R}$
Where $r$ is the distance from the centre of the charge distribution $\rho_{\mathrm{o}}$ is a constant. The electric field at an internal point $(r < R)$ is:
questions.solution:
Let us consider a spherical shell of radius $x$ and thickness $\mathrm{dx}$.
Charge on this shell $ d q=\rho .4 \pi x^2 d x=\rho_0\left(1-\frac{x}{R}\right) \cdot 4 \pi x^2 d x $ $\therefore$ Total charge in the spherical region from centre to $r(r < R)$ is $ \begin{aligned} &q=\int d q=4 \pi \rho_0 \int_0^r\left(1-\frac{x}{R}\right) x^2 d x \\ &=4 \pi \rho_0\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4 R}\right]_0^r \\ &=4 \pi \rho_0\left[\frac{r^3}{3}-\frac{r^4}{4 R}\right] \\ &=4 \pi \rho_0 r^3\left[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{r}{4 R}\right] \end{aligned} $ $\therefore$ Electric field at $\mathrm{r}, \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{r}^2}$$ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{4 \pi \rho_0 r^3}{r^2}\left[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{r}{4 R}\right] \\ &=\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{r}{3}-\frac{r^2}{4 R}\right] \end{aligned} $

questions.q: The surface charge density of a thin charged disc of radius $\mathrm{R}$ is $\sigma$. The value of the electric field at the centre of the disc is $\frac{\sigma}{2 \in_0}$. With respect to the field at the centre, the electric field along the axis at a distance $\mathrm{R}$ from the centre of the disc:
options:
reduces by $70.7 \%$

reduces by $29.3 \%$

 reduces by $9.7 \%$

reduces by $14.6 \%$
questions.solution:
Electric field intensity at the centre of the disc.

$\mathrm{E}=\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_0} \quad \text{ (given) }$Electric field along the axis at any distance $x$ from the centre of the disc

\mathrmE^{\prime}=$\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_0} \left(1-\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{x}^2+\mathrm{R}^2}}\right)From question,  \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{R} (radius of disc)

\begin{aligned}
\therefore \mathrmE^{\prime} &=\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_0} \left(1-\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{R}^2}}\right)\\
&=\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_0}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2} \mathrm{R}-\mathrm{R}}{\sqrt{2} \mathrm{R}}\right)
\end{aligned}

=\frac{4}{14} \mathrm{E}\therefore$\%$ reduction in the value of electric field

$=\frac{\left(E-\frac{4}{14} E\right) \times 100}{E}=\frac{1000}{14}$\%=70.7 \%

questions.q:
The gravitational field in a region is given by: $\vec{E}=(5 N / k g) \hat{i}+(12 N / k g) \hat{j}$
If the potential at the origin is taken to be zero, then the ratio of the potential at the points $(12 \mathrm{~m}, 0)$ and $(0,5 \mathrm{~m})$ is :
questions.solution:
From question, $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}}=5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{kg}$ and $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{y}}=12 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{kg}$
Gravitational potential
$=$ Gravitational field $\times$distance
$\therefore \mathrm{V}_{(12 \mathrm{~m}, 0)}=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}} \times 12 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}$
and $\mathrm{V}_{(0,5 \mathrm{~m})}=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{y}} \times 5 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}$
(Given : potential at the origin is zero)

\therefore $\frac{V_{(12 \mathrm{~m}, 0)}}{\mathrm{V}_{(0,5 \mathrm{~m})}}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}} \times 12}{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{y}} \times 5}=\frac{5 \times 12}{12 \times 5}=$1

& E=$\frac{k q}{r^2}$\\
& =$\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{1}{r^2} \cdot4 \pi \rho_0$ left[$\frac{5}{4}\left(\frac{r^3}{3}\right)-\frac{r^4}{4 R}\right]$\\
& $E=\frac{\rho_0 r}{4 \varepsilon_0}  $left[\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R}\right] \\
&

$

Apply shell theorem the total charge upto distance $r$ can be calculated as followed $d q=4 \pi r^2 \cdot d r . \rho$$

questions.q: An $\alpha$-particle of energy $5 \mathrm{MeV}$ is scattered through $180^{\circ}$ by a fixed uranium nucleus. The distance of the closest approach is of the order of
questions.solution:
At closest approach, all the kinetic energy of the $\alpha$-particle will converted into the potential energy of the system, K.E. = P.E.

$\begin{aligned}$& 5 $\mathrm{MeV}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}}$\\
& 5 $\times$10^6 $\times \mathrm{e}=$9 $\times$10^9 $\frac{\mathrm{Z}_1 \times \mathrm{Z}_2 \mathrm{e}^2}{\mathrm{r}}$\\
& $\mathrm{r}=\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 92 \times 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{5 \times 10^6}$\\
& \therefore $\mathrm{r}=$5.3 $\times$10^{-14} $\mathrm{~m}=$5.3 $\times$10^{-12} $\mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}$
